title: Of Fortune, Industry, and Perseverance

keywords: of the uselessness of endeavour against persistent ill fortune
full_text:
Before the tribunal of King Azadbakht, the First Wazir presented an argument on the stubborn nature of misfortune: 'Sire, when destiny decrees that a man shall experience adversity, all his clever schemes become nets to trap his feet; he who struggles against the current with frantic pride only drowns.'

Bakhtiyar stood before the throne, bowed with courtly respect, and answered with philosophical clarity:

'It is true, O King, that when the storm rages, human schemes are like leaves before the gale. But adversity is not an eternal decree; it is a season of testing designed to burn away the dross of arrogance and forge the pure gold of character.

He who surrenders to despair when misfortune strikes is like a sailor who throws away his rudder because the waves are high. The wise man does not curse the tempest; he trims his sails, anchors his soul in patient endurance, and continues his honest labor.

For every midnight has its appointed dawn, and every winter dissolves into the blossoms of spring. He who preserves his integrity through the darkest hour will find that fortune returns to crown his steadfastness with double glory, even as the history of the Merchant Who Lost His Luck demonstrates before all men.'
moral: When adversity blows like a tempest, patient endurance and honest labor outlast the storm.
